name: Giddyup End 'em Ribs
subtitle: Open whenever it is genuinely needed. Closed at all other times.
description:
There is no sign of the hours anywhere on the building, and there has never been a night when you have walked up here and found it shut. Other people report finding it shut constantly. Both accounts are held to be accurate and nobody has ever put them side by side.

Smoke first, then the room: low, long, dark wood gone darker, and the sort of warmth that a building only accumulates over centuries. Which is the trouble. The parish had the foundations dated in the sixties, out of civic pride, and the report came back with three different answers for three different courses of stone — one of them four hundred years before there was a Silvora Reefs to build in, and one of them for a material the report's author noted, in a footnote he clearly enjoyed, was not yet being manufactured.

The walls are masks. That is the thing everybody remembers about this room, and everybody remembers it wrongly, because they remember it as decoration.
revisit:
Ben is at the long table with his hands flat on it, and he greets you with his own name in the form of a question, and the question lands the way it always lands — as though he already has the answer and is being polite about the interval.

The room is warm from a fire at the cold end and warm from a smoker somewhere behind, and the smoke goes up and out through a roof that has no vent in it. Two hundred masks watch from the walls at forty different heights. The one near the door is smiling and was not smiling, and Ben has not moved, and Ben will not move, because he has told you that keeping his palms flat on that table is what keeps him where he is and he was not being figurative.

lucid.2: The smoke goes up and out through a roof that has no vent in it.
lucid.3: There are two hundred masks and there are two hundred people in Silvora Reefs, and neither of those numbers has ever needed to be counted.
lucid.4: This building is older than the town because it was written first. Everything else was worked out from here.

ambient: Ben says something about a summer you have not told anybody about — a detail, small, correct, offered in passing the way a man offers the weather — and moves on before it can become a question.
The fire settles. In the settling there is the sound of a lever being thrown at the end of a line, and a pause, and a return, and then it is a fire again and has been a fire all along.
A mask on the west wall is not where it was. The nail it was on is still in the wall, and there is no dust ring around it, and there is no dust ring where it is now either.

Somebody at the far end of the long table laughs, and eleven strangers who have never met laugh with them, and the laugh goes down the oak and arrives at your elbow as a vibration about a second later.
Ben lifts one palm off the table to reach for something, and puts it back before the reach is finished, and does not get whatever it was.

objects.name: the masks
objects.description:
They cover the walls from the wainscot to the beams, overlapping, four and five deep in places, carved in a dozen different woods by what must be a dozen different hands over what must be a very long time indeed.

And they are portraits. Not one of them is an abstraction, not one is a god or a demon or a harvest figure or any of the things a wall of masks in an old building is supposed to be. They are people, and they are people you know.

There is Darek in the corner by the door, with the drawl carved into the set of the jaw. Soliloquy over the fire, holding her chin at the exact angle she holds it. Ginny high on the west wall with her hair pinned like a threat. Asimov. Luigi. Mary Guana, half-shut and unhurried. And a bull antelope with antlers that go the wrong way at the third branch and an expression of enormous, effortful hope.

Ben's position on all this is that they are old masks. He has never disputed a single one of the resemblances. He has never once said the word 'resemblance' either, in fifty years, to anybody.
objects.repeat: There is one near the door that was not near the door. It is Darek. He is smiling in it, and he was not smiling in it, and the wood around the mouth is not fresh-cut — whatever changed, it did not change by being carved.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the masks are not carved. They are *cast* — every one taken from the same original, and then worked afterwards into difference, and the working is skilful and the original is underneath all of them and the original has your bone structure.

passive.text: The carver liked them. All of them, individually, and it shows in the small decisions — the humour left in around Darek's mouth, the tiredness allowed into Asimov's eyes. Whoever made these was fond of every single person in this town.
A dozen hands over centuries, and yet the eye-spacing is identical on every mask on this wall. Different woods, different tools, different eras, one set of measurements.

clue.title: Every mask is somebody you know
clue.text: The masks at Giddyup are portraits of living Reefers — Darek, Soliloquy, Ginny, Asimov, Luigi — carved in a dozen woods over centuries, with identical eye-spacing on every one.

clue.title: One original, worked into difference
clue.text: Under the monocle the masks are cast from a single original and worked afterwards into difference. The original has Oliver's bone structure.

check.prompt: Take one off the wall and put it on, in front of everybody, without making it a joke. The room will decide what it means about a second and a half after you do it, so get in first.
check.success:
You put it on. You do not do a voice. You do not make the face people make when they put on a mask, and the room, which had been ready to laugh, has nowhere to put the laugh and quietly keeps it.

From inside, the eyeholes line up with the room in a way that is off by a foot. These were cut for somebody standing where nobody stands — behind the counter, on the left, exactly where the proprietor has stood for eleven years.
check.failure:
You put it on and the room decides what that means before you do, and what it means is a joke, and the joke is generous and warm and completely finished with by the time it comes off.

You learn nothing except that the wood smells of smoke and that these people like you.

clue.title: Cut for one position
clue.text: The eyeholes of Giddyup's masks line up only from behind the counter, on the left, where the proprietor has stood for eleven years.

objects.name: the mask behind the others
objects.description:
Third bay from the fire, four deep, most of it behind a fisherman and a woman with a lamp. What is visible from the floor is a cheekbone, part of a jaw, and one eye.

It is you.

It is unmistakably you and it takes about a second and a half to be certain of it — and in that second and a half there is a stage where it is not you and is somebody with your cheekbone, a stranger who happens to be built the same way, and that stage is the part that stays with you afterwards and comes back at four in the morning.

The features are not quite in the arrangement you keep them in. Nothing is missing. Nothing has been added, and nothing has been exaggerated the way a carver exaggerates when he is working from memory or from fondness.

Everything has been moved about a sixteenth of an inch. In different directions. By somebody who knew exactly what they were doing, and had a reason for each one, and had the skill to stop precisely where they stopped.
objects.repeat: You have moved the fisherman aside twice now. Both times it has been back over the eye by the time you looked again, and both times Ben has been at the long table with his palms flat and his eyes somewhere else entirely, and both times he has said nothing at all about it.

lucid.3: The sixteenth of an inch is not random. Every feature has been moved toward the mirror-image position and stopped short of it.
lucid.4: It is not a warped face. It is a face that was going to be reversed and was interrupted.

objects.monocle: Through the gold the mask is whole and unobstructed and facing you, and the fisherman and the woman with the lamp are somewhere else entirely, and on the inside of the mask — the side that goes against a face — somebody has written, small, in pencil: NOT YET.

check.prompt: Move the fisherman properly. Not a nudge and not a lean — lift it off the nail, put it on the table, and look at the thing behind it with the whole of your attention and nothing held back for comfort.
check.success:
The fisherman comes off the nail. The woman with the lamp comes off the nail. You put them on the long table, one either side of Ben's hands, and Ben does not move them and does not stop you and does not look.

And it is your face, complete, and it is wrong in the way described, and it is not a wrongness of craft. Every displacement is toward the mirror image. The nose leans a sixteenth the other way, the jaw sits a sixteenth the other way, the parting is on the other side by a sixteenth — and none of them arrives, all of them stop short, and the effect is of a reversal that somebody began and did not finish.

Ben says, to the table: "That one's older than the others, and it ain't. Both. I've had it up thirty years and I've never hung it and I've never took it down."
check.failure:
The fisherman is on a nail that has been there since the war and it does not want to come off it, and you get it half up and the whole bay shifts an inch and something at the back knocks, and you put it back.

Ben has not looked up. Ben's hands are flat on the long table and he says, at a normal volume, to nobody: "Some things is hung and some things is just up there."

clue.title: A reversal that stopped short
clue.text: The hidden mask is Oliver's face with every feature displaced a sixteenth of an inch toward its mirror image and stopping short. Ben has had it thirty years, has never hung it, and has never taken it down.

clue.title: NOT YET
clue.text: On the inside of the hidden mask — the side that goes against a face — somebody has written in small pencil: NOT YET.

objects.name: the exposed foundation course
objects.description:
By the cold end of the room somebody has taken up three boards and never put them back, and under them is the top course of the original footing, and beside it in a frame on the wall is the parish's dating report from 1963, kept up because Ben thinks it is funny.

Three courses. Three answers. The bottom one predates Silvora Reefs by four hundred years, which the report handles calmly. The middle one is unremarkable. The top one is a cement compound that the report's author identifies, correctly and at some length and with obvious delight, as not yet being in production.

The conclusion of the report reads: THE BUILDING IS THEREFORE OF INDETERMINATE BUT UNDOUBTED ANTIQUITY. Somebody in the parish office has written OK in the margin.
objects.repeat: The OK in the margin is in a hand you have started to be able to pick out of a crowd — the same slight backward lean, the same way of closing an O without quite closing it.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the three courses are three drafts. The bottom is the earliest and it is the roughest and it has the most life in it. The middle is competent. The top is the newest and is the most careful and is holding up the least.

passive.text: A building cannot be built out of a material that does not exist yet. But a building can be *described* as being built out of one, by somebody who knows the material, who is not writing in 1963.

'Indeterminate but undoubted antiquity.' The author had three contradictory results and produced a sentence that is true of all three. That is not incompetence. That is a professional at the end of his patience doing something rather beautiful.

clue.title: Three courses, three centuries
clue.text: Giddyup's foundations date to three incompatible periods, one predating the town by four hundred years and one using a cement not yet manufactured in 1963.

clue.title: Three drafts
clue.text: Under the monocle the three foundation courses are three drafts — the oldest roughest and most alive, the newest most careful and holding up least.

check.prompt: The building sits on something older than the building and somebody took three boards up to look at it and never put them back. Get underneath and read the mechanism rather than the report.
check.success:
Under the floor the joists rest on a frame, and the frame is not a foundation. It has bearings in it, and a track, and the track is circular.

This building is mounted to turn. It has not turned — the grease is undisturbed — but it was built by somebody who expected it to, and it is aimed, currently, at the harbour.
check.failure:
Joists, a frame, and a very great deal of very old grease.

Whatever the frame is for, it declines to say from this angle, with this light, with this back — and there is about nine inches of clearance under the boards and a man of your age gets one attempt at that per evening.

clue.title: Mounted to turn
clue.text: Giddyup sits on a circular track with bearings. It has never turned, but it was built to, and it is aimed at the harbour.

objects.name: the long table
objects.description:
One piece of oak, twenty-two feet, black with a century of hands and shining along the edges where forearms go.

Ben sits at the middle of the long side with both palms flat on it. That is how he sits and it is the only way you have ever seen him sit, and it is not a mannerism — he told you once, without being asked and without any particular weight, that it keeps him where he is, and then he changed the subject in the manner of a man who has said the true thing and does not intend to say it twice.

There are names carved into the underside. You found them by dropping a fork and going after it. Hundreds of them, running the whole length, cut small and neat and unmistakably by the same tool at the same pressure — over a century of names, in one hand, which is not a thing a century can contain.

Each one has a date beside it. The dates are not births and they are not deaths.

The most recent name is yours. The date beside it is four days after you came out of the harbour, which has not happened yet.
objects.repeat: You check the date again. It is one day closer than it was and the carving has not been recut; there is no fresh cut, no dust, no change in the colour of the wood inside the stroke. The number is simply different.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the dates are not dates. They are page numbers. Yours is high and it is not the highest, and the highest one belongs to a name you cannot read because the tool slipped, or because it has not been decided.

passive.text: One tool. Hundreds of names, over what the wear says is a century, and one tool, and the same pressure. Nobody's hand stays that steady for a century.
Ben knows they are there. Ben has sat with his palms flat on this table for fifty years directly above a list with his own name in it, and he has never once mentioned it, and he has never once moved.

clue.title: A list with a date beside your name
clue.text: Hundreds of names are carved into the underside of Ben's table in a single tool over a century. Each has a date that is neither birth nor death. The most recent is Oliver's, and it is in the future, and it moves closer.

clue.title: They are page numbers
clue.text: Under the monocle the dates carved beside each name are page numbers. Oliver's is high but not highest. The highest belongs to a name the tool slipped on, or that has not been decided.

check.prompt: The long table seats eleven and nine of them are strangers to each other, and all of them are warm and fed and halfway down a drink. Get the table talking about the night the harbour lit up without asking it to.
check.success:
You do not ask. You put the subject down in the middle of the table like a dish and let them serve themselves.

Within four minutes eleven people are arguing about a night none of them will place, and the argument has a shape: everybody remembers the light, nobody remembers the sound, and two of them remember being outside for it and having no reason to have been.
check.failure: You put the subject down and it sits there. Somebody asks whether you mean the fireworks. Somebody else says there were no fireworks. The table agrees pleasantly that there were no fireworks and returns to the ribs, and the moment is gone and cannot be put down twice.

clue.title: The light, and no sound
clue.text: Eleven strangers at Giddyup all remember a light over the harbour and none remember a sound. Two remember being outside for it without reason.

objects.name: the arrangement of the masks
objects.description:
Not the masks themselves. The *hanging* of them — what has been put at eye level and what has been put above it, what is grouped and what has been given a foot of clear wall on either side, which faces have been placed where they can see one another and which two have been separated by the width of a beam.

It is not by size. There is a small one high and a large one low within a yard of each other. It is not by wood, or by age, or by the hand that carved them, and it is emphatically not by any scheme of decoration a person would arrive at while trying to fill a wall.

Somebody has done this deliberately, over a very long period, revising as they went. There are nail holes that have nothing on them any more, and nail holes that have been filled and painted over, and one bay near the fire where the wall has been made good three separate times.
objects.repeat: The arrangement is holding, except in the third bay, where it never quite does. Two masks there have swapped since Tuesday and the eyelines through that bay now converge about four inches further from the fire than they did.
objects.monocle:
Through the gold there is a seating plan under the masks: ruled, lettered, with a key in the corner and the fire marked as a fixed point.

It has been revised many times. The rubbings-out are still there under the current version, and so are the versions under those.

And every single revision moves somebody nearer the fire. Nobody has ever been moved away from it. Sixty years of a man quietly shifting two hundred people closer to the warm end of a room they cannot leave.

clue.title: Arranged, not accumulated
clue.text: The Giddyup masks are hung by no rule of size, wood or age — but by eyeline and grouping, deliberately, over a very long period.

check.prompt: Two hundred portraits, hung by somebody, in an order, over decades, with revisions. Stop counting the faces and work out what the room is *for*.
check.success:
Not a gallery. A gallery faces its pictures outward at whoever comes in, and these do not face the door.

They face the room. All of them, at their various heights, angled a few degrees off the wall so that their sightlines converge — and they converge low, and near the fire, at the place a man would be if he were sitting at the middle of the long side of the table with his palms flat on it.

It is not a trophy room and it is not a shrine. It is a room built so that one person can be looked at, kindly, and at length, by every single person he has ever made — and it has been assembled by somebody who could not say that out loud and has been saying it in carpentry for thirty years.
check.failure: Two hundred faces at forty heights, and every grouping you propose holds for about nine masks before the tenth ruins it. There is an order here. It is not going to be found from the middle of the floor with the fire this bright.

clue.title: A room for being looked at kindly
clue.text: The masks' sightlines converge on the seat at the middle of the long table. Giddyup is not a gallery or a shrine — it is a room arranged so one man can be witnessed, at length, by everyone he made.

exits.outside_inn: down and seaward, to a building with its own weather
exits.cheeses_thrice: along the ridge, toward an oven that can be smelled from here
